title: Semisimplicity tested by commutative normal subgroups over a perfect field
statement:
Let $k$ be a perfect field [def-weil-field], meaning that every irreducible polynomial over $k$ is separable (has no repeated root in an algebraic closure [def-weil-algebraic-closure]). Let $G$ be a smooth geometrically connected affine $k$-group scheme of finite type [def-sc-group-scheme, def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. Geometrically connected means connected after extension to an algebraic closure [def-weil-connected-scheme]. Closed normal subgroup inclusions have the meaning of [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. Then the following are equivalent:
(1) $G$ is semisimple: over an algebraic closure $\bar k$ it has no nontrivial smooth connected solvable normal closed subgroup scheme. Here solvable means that the successive scheme-theoretic derived subgroups eventually become trivial, and a derived subgroup is the smallest closed subgroup through which the commutator morphism $(x,y)\mapsto xyx^{-1}y^{-1}$ factors.
(2) For every smooth connected commutative affine $k$-group scheme $N$ of finite type and every closed normal subgroup inclusion $N\hookrightarrow G$, the identity morphism $\operatorname{Spec}k\to N$ is an isomorphism.
No characteristic-zero, splitness or reductivity hypothesis is assumed; the trivial group is allowed.

source.place: Proposition 19.3 and its proof, printed p.398, with geometric semisimplicity in 6.44 (p.135), radical base change in Proposition 19.1 (p.397), and Proposition 19.2(a) (p.398). The test explicitly ranges over affine finite-type subgroup schemes, as all closed subgroups of G are such. No Stacks tag states this algebraic-group criterion.

proof.text: First compare the two descriptions of solvability. Given a finite series $H=H_0\supseteq\cdots\supseteq H_s=1$ whose commutators in $H_i$ lie in $H_{i+1}$, minimality of the derived subgroup gives $D^i(H)\subseteq H_i$ by induction: the commutators of $D^i(H)$ lie in $H_{i+1}$. Conversely, a terminating derived series is such a series because the derived quotients are commutative. Thus the finite-series solvability in [lem-sfb-solvable-normal-subgroup-products] is exactly that in this item. The derived subgroups here exist for smooth connected groups; [lem-sfb-solvable-normal-subgroup-products] makes them geometrically connected, and [lem-sfb-derived-commutator-word-arbitrary-field] supplies the next smooth geometrically connected derived subgroup at each stage.

source.place: Definition 6.26 and Proposition 6.30, pp.131--132; Corollary 6.19, p.129

proof.text: Assume (1), and take $N$ as in (2). By [lem-sfb-solvable-normal-subgroup-products], its extension $N_{\bar k}$ is smooth and connected. Its closed inclusion, normality and commutativity persist after extension: evaluate the subgroup identities on every commutative $\bar k$-algebra, regarded as a $k$-algebra [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. The commutator is identity-valued, so its derived subgroup is trivial and it is solvable. Hence (1) forces $N_{\bar k}=1$. For completeness this implies $N=1$ scheme-theoretically: for the augmentation $\epsilon:k[N]\to k$, write $k[N]=k\oplus I$ as vector spaces, where $I=\ker\epsilon$. Tensoring gives $\bar k[N_{\bar k}]=\bar k\oplus(I\otimes_k\bar k)$, so $I\otimes_k\bar k=0$. A nonzero vector in $I$ extends to a basis and stays nonzero after field extension, so $I=0$. Thus the augmentation is an isomorphism and its corresponding identity section $\operatorname{Spec}k\to N$ is an isomorphism.

source.place: Proposition 19.3, first paragraph of proof, p.398; Proposition 1.36 on connected group varieties

proof.text: Construct $R\subseteq G$ by choosing a smooth connected solvable normal closed subgroup of largest dimension. Such a choice exists: the trivial group is a candidate and the candidate dimensions are nonnegative integers bounded by $\dim G$. For any other candidate $N$, [lem-sfb-solvable-normal-subgroup-products] supplies a candidate $RN$ containing $R,N$. If $R\subsetneq RN$, its strict-inclusion dimension clause contradicts maximality. Therefore $RN=R$, whence $N\subseteq R$. This proves precisely the largest-subgroup hypothesis needed below, without assuming reductivity.

source.place: 6.44, p.135, via Proposition 6.42 and Lemma 6.41, p.134

proof.text: Because $k$ is perfect, the minimal polynomial over $k$ of every element of $\bar k$ is separable; hence $\bar k/k$ is separable algebraic. Apply [lem-sfb-solvable-radical-separable-base-change] to the $R$ just constructed and $K=\bar k$. It says that $R_{\bar k}$ is a smooth connected solvable normal subgroup containing every such subgroup of $G_{\bar k}$. If $R=1$, this proves (1) directly. Consequently, to prove (2) implies (1), it remains to exclude $R\ne1$.

Assume (2) and $R\ne1$. Put $R_0=R$ and $R_{i+1}=D(R_i)$. Inductively [lem-sfb-derived-commutator-word-arbitrary-field] gives smooth geometrically connected affine finite-type closed subgroups. At the base $R$ is geometrically connected by [lem-sfb-solvable-normal-subgroup-products]. Each $R_i$ is normal in $G$: this holds for $i=0$ by construction; if it holds for $i$, for every commutative $k$-algebra $A$ and $g\in G(A)$, conjugation restricts to an $A$-group automorphism of $(R_i)_A$. By [lem-sfb-derived-subgroup-universal-characteristic] it preserves $(R_{i+1})_A$. Evaluating this restriction on $A$-points proves normality of $R_{i+1}$ for all $A$, exactly [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. Since $R$ is solvable, choose the least $s$ with $R_s=1$; then $s\ge1$ and $R_{s-1}\ne1$.

source.place: Proposition 19.3, converse proof, p.398; Corollary 6.19(b),(e), pp.129--130; derived series before Proposition 6.30, p.132

proof.text: Take $N=R_{s-1}$ with its composite closed inclusion in $G$. Its commutator morphism factors through $D(N)=R_s=1$, so for every $A$ and $x,y\in N(A)$ one has $xyx^{-1}y^{-1}=e$, equivalently $xy=yx$. Thus $N$ is commutative, and step 5 already gives smoothness, connectedness, affineness, finite type and normality. Condition (2) makes its identity section an isomorphism, contradicting $R_{s-1}\ne1$. Therefore $R=1$ and step 4 proves (1). If $G=1$, the forward argument and the choice $R=1$ apply without selecting any nontrivial derived term.
